[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 18: Misleading or deceptive conduct | compilation 2026-08-27
18 Misleading or deceptive conduct 1 A person must not, in trade or commerce, engage in conduct that is misleading or deceptive or is likely to mislead or deceive. 2 Nothing in Part 3-1 (which is about unfair practices) limits by implication subsection (1). Note: For rules relating to representations as to the country of origin of goods, see Part 5-3.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 18.

Rule: A person must not, in trade or commerce, engage in conduct that is misleading or deceptive or likely to mislead or deceive. [1]

Meaning: The wording includes likely deception, so the prohibition is not confined to conduct described as having already deceived someone. [1]

Limits: The provision concerns conduct in trade or commerce. This extract does not specify a dollar penalty or decide whether particular conduct breaches the rule. [1]

<evidence>
[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 24: Meaning of unfair | compilation 2026-08-27
24 Meaning of unfair 1 (1) A term of a consumer contract or small business contract is unfair if: a it would cause a significant imbalance in the parties’ rights and obligations arising under the contract; and b it is not reasonably necessary in order to protect the legitimate interests of the party who would be advantaged by the term; and c it would cause detriment (whether financial or otherwise) to a party if it were to be applied or relied on. 2 In determining whether a term of a contract is unfair under subsection (1), a court may take into account such matters as it thinks relevant, but must take into account the following: a the extent to which the term is transparent; b the contract as a whole. 3 (3) A term is transparent if the term is: a expressed in reasonably plain language; and b legible; and c presented clearly; and d readily available to any party affected by the term. 4 For the purposes of subsection (1)(b), a term of a contract is presumed not to be reasonably necessary in order to protect the legitimate interests of the party who would be advantaged by the term, unless that party proves otherwise.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 24.

Rule: The term must cause a significant imbalance, not be reasonably necessary to protect the advantaged party's legitimate interests, and cause detriment if applied or relied on. [1]

Meaning: All three conditions form the test. The court must consider transparency and the contract as a whole, alongside any other relevant matters. [1]

Limits: Transparency means plain language, legibility, clear presentation and availability. The advantaged party must rebut the presumption that the term is not reasonably necessary; transparency alone does not decide the three-part test. [1]

<evidence>
[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 54: Guarantee as to acceptable quality | compilation 2026-08-27
54 Guarantee as to acceptable quality 1 If: a a person supplies, in trade or commerce, goods to a consumer; and b the supply does not occur by way of sale by auction; there is a guarantee that the goods are of acceptable quality. 2 (2) Goods are of acceptable quality if they are as: a fit for all the purposes for which goods of that kind are commonly supplied; and b acceptable in appearance and finish; and c free from defects; and d safe; and e durable; as a reasonable consumer fully acquainted with the state and condition of the goods (including any hidden defects of the goods), would regard as acceptable having regard to the matters in subsection (3). 3 The matters for the purposes of subsection (2) are: a the nature of the goods; and b the price of the goods (if relevant); and c any statements made about the goods on any packaging or label on the goods; and d any representation made about the goods by the supplier or manufacturer of the goods; and e any other relevant circumstances relating to the supply of the goods. 4 If: a goods supplied to a consumer are not of acceptable quality; and b the only reason or reasons why they are not of acceptable quality were specifically drawn to the consumer’s attention before the consumer agreed to the supply; the goods are taken to be of acceptable quality. 5 If: a goods are displayed for sale or hire; and b the goods would not be of acceptable quality if they were supplied to a consumer; the reason or reasons why they are not of acceptable quality are taken, for the purposes of subsection (4), to have been specifically drawn to a consumer’s attention if those reasons were disclosed on a written notice that was displayed with the goods and that was transparent. 6 Goods do not fail to be of acceptable quality if: a the consumer to whom they are supplied causes them to become of unacceptable quality, or fails to take reasonable steps to prevent them from becoming of unacceptable quality; and b they are damaged by abnormal use. 7 Goods do not fail to be of acceptable quality if: a the consumer acquiring the goods examines them before the consumer agrees to the supply of the goods; and b the examination ought reasonably to have revealed that the goods were not of acceptable quality.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 54.

Rule: Goods must be fit for their common purposes, acceptable in appearance and finish, free from defects, safe and durable, to the standard a reasonable consumer fully acquainted with their condition would regard as acceptable. [1]

Meaning: The assessment considers the goods' nature, relevant price, packaging or label statements, supplier or manufacturer representations, and other relevant supply circumstances. [1]

Limits: The section excludes auction supplies. It also qualifies the rule for defects specifically disclosed before agreement, damage caused by abnormal use in the stated circumstances, and examination that ought to reveal the problem. It supplies no universal product lifespan. [1]

<evidence>
[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 55: Guarantee as to fitness for any disclosed purpose etc. | compilation 2026-08-27
55 Guarantee as to fitness for any disclosed purpose etc. 1 If: a (a) a person (the supplier) supplies, in trade or commerce, goods to a consumer; and b the supply does not occur by way of sale by auction; there is a guarantee that the goods are reasonably fit for any disclosed purpose, and for any purpose for which the supplier represents that they are reasonably fit. 2 (2) A disclosed purpose is a particular purpose (whether or not that purpose is a purpose for which the goods are commonly supplied) for which the goods are being acquired by the consumer and that: a the consumer makes known, expressly or by implication, to: i the supplier; or ii a person by whom any prior negotiations or arrangements in relation to the acquisition of the goods were conducted or made; or b the consumer makes known to the manufacturer of the goods either directly or through the supplier or the person referred to in paragraph (a)(ii). 3 This section does not apply if the circumstances show that the consumer did not rely on, or that it was unreasonable for the consumer to rely on, the skill or judgment of the supplier, the person referred to in subsection (2)(a)(ii) or the manufacturer, as the case may be.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 55.

Rule: Goods supplied in trade or commerce to a consumer, outside auction supplies, must be reasonably fit for a disclosed purpose and a purpose the supplier represents they are reasonably fit for. [1]

Meaning: A disclosed purpose can be made known expressly or by implication to the supplier, a person conducting prior negotiations, or the manufacturer as described in the section. [1]

Limits: The guarantee does not apply if the circumstances show no reliance, or unreasonable reliance, on the relevant supplier's, negotiator's or manufacturer's skill or judgment. A particular dispute still requires its facts. [1]

[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 60: Guarantee as to due care and skill | compilation 2026-08-27
60 Guarantee as to due care and skill If a person supplies, in trade or commerce, services to a consumer, there is a guarantee that the services will be rendered with due care and skill.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 60.

Rule: Where services are supplied in trade or commerce to a consumer, there is a guarantee that they will be rendered with due care and skill. [1]

Meaning: The passage concerns the care and skill used in performing the service. It does not say the consumer must disclose a particular purpose for this guarantee to apply. [1]

Limits: This short provision states its trade-or-commerce and consumer scope. It does not set a fixed completion date or determine the result of an individual claim. [1]

<evidence>
[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 61: Guarantees as to fitness for a particular purpose etc. | compilation 2026-08-27
61 Guarantees as to fitness for a particular purpose etc. 1 If: a (a) a person (the supplier) supplies, in trade or commerce, services to a consumer; and b the consumer, expressly or by implication, makes known to the supplier any particular purpose for which the services are being acquired by the consumer; there is a guarantee that the services, and any product resulting from the services, will be reasonably fit for that purpose. 2 If: a (a) a person (the supplier) supplies, in trade or commerce, services to a consumer; and b the consumer makes known, expressly or by implication, to: i the supplier; or ii a person by whom any prior negotiations or arrangements in relation to the acquisition of the services were conducted or made; the result that the consumer wishes the services to achieve; there is a guarantee that the services, and any product resulting from the services, will be of such a nature, and quality, state or condition, that they might reasonably be expected to achieve that result. 3 This section does not apply if the circumstances show that the consumer did not rely on, or that it was unreasonable for the consumer to rely on, the skill or judgment of the supplier. 4 This section does not apply to a supply of services of a professional nature by a qualified architect or engineer.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 61.

Rule: When the consumer makes a particular purpose known, services and their resulting product must be reasonably fit for it. A disclosed desired result also attracts the stated guarantee about their nature, quality, state or condition. [1]

Meaning: This provision concerns a purpose or result made known expressly or by implication, rather than merely the care used while doing the work. [1]

Limits: The section does not apply where the consumer did not rely, or unreasonably relied, on the supplier's skill or judgment. It also excludes professional services supplied by a qualified architect or engineer. [1]

<evidence>
[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 64: Guarantees not to be excluded etc. by contract | compilation 2026-08-27
64 Guarantees not to be excluded etc. by contract 1 A term of a contract (including a term that is not set out in the contract but is incorporated in the contract by another term of the contract) is void to the extent that the term purports to exclude, restrict or modify, or has the effect of excluding, restricting or modifying: a the application of all or any of the provisions of this Division; or b the exercise of a right conferred by such a provision; or c any liability of a person for a failure to comply with a guarantee that applies under this Division to a supply of goods or services. 2 A term of a contract is not taken, for the purposes of this section, to exclude, restrict or modify the application of a provision of this Division unless the term does so expressly or is inconsistent with the provision.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 64.

Rule: A contract term is void to the extent it purports, or has the effect, of excluding, restricting or modifying the relevant guarantees, rights, or liability for non-compliance. [1]

Meaning: The rule includes incorporated terms as well as terms written out in the contract. The wording addresses the offending extent of a term rather than declaring the whole contract void. [1]

Limits: Under this section, a term is not treated as excluding, restricting or modifying a provision unless it does so expressly or is inconsistent with it. The extract alone does not resolve every possible limitation-of-liability question. [1]

<evidence>
[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 260: When a failure to comply with a guarantee is a major failure | compilation 2026-08-27
260 When a failure to comply with a guarantee is a major failure 1 (1) A failure to comply with a guarantee referred to in section 259(1)(b) that applies to a supply of goods is a major failure if: a the goods would not have been acquired by a reasonable consumer fully acquainted with the nature and extent of the failure; or b the goods depart in one or more significant respects: i if they were supplied by description—from that description; or ii if they were supplied by reference to a sample or demonstration model—from that sample or demonstration model; or c the goods are substantially unfit for a purpose for which goods of the same kind are commonly supplied and they cannot, easily and within a reasonable time, be remedied to make them fit for such a purpose; or d the goods are unfit for a disclosed purpose that was made known to: i the supplier of the goods; or ii a person by whom any prior negotiations or arrangements in relation to the acquisition of the goods were conducted or made; and they cannot, easily and within a reasonable time, be remedied to make them fit for such a purpose; or e the goods are not of acceptable quality because they are unsafe. 2 (2) A failure to comply with a guarantee referred to in section 259(1)(b) that applies to a supply of goods is also a major failure if: a the failure is one of 2 or more failures to comply with a guarantee referred to in section 259(1)(b) that apply to the supply; and b the goods would not have been acquired by a reasonable consumer fully acquainted with the nature and extent of those failures, taken as a whole. Note: The multiple failures do not need to relate to the same guarantee. 3 Subsection (2) applies regardless of whether the consumer has taken action under section 259 in relation to any of the failures.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 260.

Rule: Major-failure grounds include the reasonable-consumer acquisition test, significant departure from description or sample, the stated unfitness grounds, and goods not of acceptable quality because they are unsafe. [1]

Meaning: The section also addresses two or more guarantee failures where a reasonable consumer fully aware of them, taken together, would not have acquired the goods. [1]

Limits: The common-purpose and disclosed-purpose unfitness grounds include inability to remedy easily and within a reasonable time. Multiple failures need not concern the same guarantee, and prior consumer action does not prevent the combined-failures test. [1]

<evidence>
[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 261: How suppliers may remedy a failure to comply with a guarantee | compilation 2026-08-27
261 How suppliers may remedy a failure to comply with a guarantee If, under section 259(2)(a), a consumer requires a supplier of goods to remedy a failure to comply with a guarantee referred to in section 259(1)(b), the supplier may comply with the requirement: a if the failure relates to title—by curing any defect in title; or b if the failure does not relate to title—by repairing the goods; or c by replacing the goods with goods of an identical type; or d by refunding: i any money paid by the consumer for the goods; and ii an amount that is equal to the value of any other consideration provided by the consumer for the goods.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 261.

Rule: The listed methods are curing a title defect, repairing goods where the failure does not concern title, replacing goods with an identical type, or refunding money and the value of other consideration. [1]

Meaning: These are the ways the supplier may comply when the consumer requires a remedy under section 259(2)(a). The provision distinguishes title defects from other failures. [1]

Limits: This section states the methods within that cross-referenced requirement. It does not establish that every consumer can demand every method in every dispute or supply a fixed repair deadline. [1]

<evidence>
[1] Australian Consumer Law — s 263: Consequences of rejecting goods | compilation 2026-08-27
263 Consequences of rejecting goods 1 This section applies if, under section 259, a consumer notifies a supplier of goods that the consumer rejects the goods. 2 The consumer must return the goods to the supplier unless: a the goods have already been returned to, or retrieved by, the supplier; or b the goods cannot be returned, removed or transported without significant cost to the consumer because of: i the nature of the failure to comply with the guarantee to which the rejection relates; or ii the size or height, or method of attachment, of the goods. 3 If subsection (2)(b) applies, the supplier must, within a reasonable time, collect the goods at the supplier’s expense. 4 The supplier must, in accordance with an election made by the consumer: a refund: i any money paid by the consumer for the goods; and ii an amount that is equal to the value of any other consideration provided by the consumer for the goods; or b replace the rejected goods with goods of the same type, and of similar value, if such goods are reasonably available to the supplier. 5 The supplier cannot satisfy subsection (4)(a) by permitting the consumer to acquire goods from the supplier. 6 If the property in the rejected goods had passed to the consumer before the rejection was notified, the property in those goods revests in the supplier on the notification of the rejection.
</evidence>

Question: Explain the qualifications and meaning of section 263.

Rule: When the consumer notifies rejection under section 259, the supplier must follow the consumer's election of a refund of money and other consideration, or replacement goods of the same type and similar value if reasonably available. [1]

Meaning: The consumer generally returns the goods. Where return, removal or transport would impose significant cost for the stated reasons, the supplier must collect them at its expense within a reasonable time. [1]

Limits: The collection exception refers to the failure's nature or the goods' size, height or attachment. A refund cannot be satisfied by letting the consumer acquire goods from the supplier. The provision assumes a rejection under section 259; it does not create an unconditional right to reject. [1]
